stories.title: Enphase and Infineon deploy 900V GaN switches in solid-state transformers designed for AI data centers
stories.summary: Claim the deployment is a "world's first"
stories.title_zh: Enphase和Infineon在专为AI数据中心设计的固态变压器中部署900V GaN开关
stories.content:
Electrical equipment manufacturer Enphase Energy has partnered with German semiconductor firm Infineon Technologies to deploy what it calls “the world’s first” 900 Volt gallium nitride (GaN) monolithic bidirectional switch (BDS) devices within Enphase's solid-state transformer power modules.

The partners claim the deployment will play a crucial role in scaling Enphase’s IQ Solid-State Transformer (IQ SST), designed for the AI data center sector.

According to Enphase, the BDS devices will allow Enphase to continue using components rated below 1kV, expanding design options for high-performance power conversion that typically rely on silicon carbide (SiC) technology. The company also claims that, within an SST, the switches will reduce switching losses and require fewer components in the power path.

The company said that on the DC side, higher-voltage unidirectional switch (UDS) devices would enable unipolar 800V power generation rather than split +/-400V buses, and support future 1,500VDC bus architectures through split +/-750V generation with fewer switches and lower bridge losses.

"Enphase asks more of our technology than almost anyone, and medium-voltage solid-state transformers are exactly where high-voltage GaN proves its value," said Johannes Schoiswohl, senior vice president and head of GaN Systems Business Line at Infineon. "Moving past 650V lets system designers strip cost and loss out of the architecture rather than optimizing around it."

"GaN is not new to us. It has been running in Enphase IQ9 Microinverters in the field, and that field data is why we trust it in a megawatt-class system," said Hans van Antwerpen, senior vice president and chief technology officer at Enphase Energy.

"Moving to 900V gives us more voltage headroom without giving up high-frequency switching, and it allows us to stay with components rated below 1kV while reducing the number of converters in the system. Fewer parts in the power path means higher efficiency and fewer things that can fail."

The 900V GaN BDS devices have been successfully tested and are now being integrated into IQ SST development builds, with production qualification expected to follow.

SSTs are growing in popularity across the data center sector, with several major firms signing deals with providers over recent months. Earlier this month, Vantage inked a deal with SST manufacturer Heron Power to secure more than 1GW of the company’s SST’s to deploy across its hyperscale data center portfolio. Heron has also partnered with Crusoe.

Infineon has also partnered with other manufacturers on the technology. Last month, the firm signed a deal with Eaton to provide the company with silicon carbide (SiC) power devices for deployment in the power management firm’s medium-voltage SST platform.

stories.title: US voters turning against data centers raises risks for Asian suppliers
stories.summary: Growing political opposition to data center development among US voters is creating ripple effects for Asian suppliers and investors. The backlash, driven by concerns over power consumption, water usage, and housing costs, threatens to slow North American expansion and redirect capital flows toward APAC markets.
stories.why_it_matters: Asian data center markets could see accelerated investment if US expansion faces regulatory and community headwinds, but they also risk importing similar political dynamics. The shift also intensifies competition for limited APAC capacity, potentially driving up land and power costs in Singapore, Japan, and Australia.

stories.summary: It plans to spend about US$825 billion in the future on AI, data centres and cloud computing

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.title_zh: Meta拟筹集高达950亿美元股权以资助高成本的AI扩张
stories.content:
It plans to spend about US$825 billion in the future on AI, data centres and cloud computing

META Platforms said on Monday (Oct 26) it plans to raise up to US$95 billion in equity to fund its costly AI-related expansion of data centres, cloud computing power and other infrastructure.

The company launched public offerings of about US$35 billion in common stock and convertible preferred stock. It also said it plans to launch a separate at-the-market share sale programme of up to US$60 billion after its new non-voting Class C shares begin trading, which is expected in the first quarter of 2027.

Meta has stepped up spending on data centres, computing capacity and AI products to compete with rival AI heavyweights OpenAI and Anthropic.

The social media company had cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities of US$82.45 billion, slightly exceeding its long-term debt of US$80.92 billion as of Sep 30, according to its quarterly filing from last week.

The company has committed to spend about US$825 billion in the future, primarily driven by its growing investments in data centres, AI-related infrastructure and cloud computing power.

Meta said chip companies Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom have expressed interest in purchasing up to US$5 billion of Meta’s Class A common stock in the offering.

Last week, Meta raised the lower end of its annual spending forecast, now expecting capital expenditure to be between US$135 billion and US$145 billion this year, up from US$130 billion to US$145 billion expected previously.

Meta reported a US$2.12 billion cash burn in the third quarter, marking its first negative free cash flow in over ten years, compared with a positive cash flow of US$10.63 billion a year ago.

The company reported third-quarter revenue of US$64.6 billion, ahead of Wall Street estimates of US$63.37 billion. It also projected fourth-quarter revenue between US$73 billion and US$76 billion. REUTERS

stories.content:
Energy systems and compute power must be planned together

ARTIFICIAL intelligence is often discussed as a digital revolution. But every AI service ultimately depends on physical infrastructure: chips, power systems, cooling equipment, networks and electricity.

For Singapore, this matters because power, land, water and grid capacity are constrained. The issue is not only how much electricity AI data centres will use, but also how quickly high-energy-demand facilities can come online compared with the time needed to expand electricity infrastructure.

The Energy Market Authority (EMA) expects Singapore’s peak electricity demand to grow by 2.9 to 6.5 per cent annually over the next decade, with data centres and semiconductor manufacturing among the drivers.

A reliable, diversified and renewable energy supply remains essential. But Singapore should also plan its power grid and the energy-demanding infrastructure as one connected system.

## Beyond power usage effectiveness

Singapore’s second “Data Centre – Call for Application”, which was launched in December 2025, requires new projects to achieve a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.25 or better at full IT load, adopt best-in-class IT energy-efficiency standards and source at least half their electricity from eligible green-energy pathways.

PUE measures the ratio of a data centre’s total energy use to that of its IT equipment. A PUE of 1.25 means servers using one unit of electricity need another 0.25 unit for cooling and other services.

A 2026 survey by the Uptime Institute showed a global industry average annual PUE of 1.52, holding steady from 2025 due to legacy infrastructure, even as high-density AI deployments accelerate. But this measured average is not directly comparable with Singapore’s full-load target.

PUE is useful but limited. It tells us how much additional energy a data centre consumes beyond its IT equipment. It does not tell us how effectively that IT electricity is turned into useful computing.

For Singapore, the more important question is how much useful compute and economic value can be obtained from each constrained megawatt while managing carbon emissions, water consumption and reliability.

Other measures include useful computing output per kilowatt-hour (kWh), how fully AI chips are used, water consumed per unit of IT electricity and associated carbon emissions.

The Digital Infrastructure Bill, passed in October, provides for sustainability licensing of data centres with at least 3 megawatts (MW) of critical IT load. By extending the regulatory framework to new and existing facilities, it reinforces the importance of improving the performance of Singapore’s existing data centres, not only building more efficient new ones.

## Cooling efficiency is key

Improving computing efficiency requires looking at the whole chain: chip efficiency, processor utilisation, software, power conversion, cooling and workload scheduling.

Cooling is becoming especially important. A rack of AI servers can draw more than 100 kilowatts (kW). At a steady 100 kW, that is 2,400 kWh per day or 72,000 kWh over 30 days – equivalent to the monthly use of about 270 three-room public housing flats, assuming 267 kWh each.

Actual consumption varies.

Air cooling at such densities is difficult; liquid cooling removes heat closer to processors and may reduce cooling energy while enabling higher computing density.

Singapore’s national benchmark SS 726:2026 is therefore timely. Launched in August, it is the world’s first standard specifically for liquid cooling in tropical data centres, covering design, commissioning, operation and maintenance.

But liquid cooling does not make heat disappear. The heat must still be rejected outdoors, and lowering electricity consumption by using substantially more water is not necessarily a good trade-off for Singapore. Energy and water need to be optimised together.

By reducing cooling energy consumption and improving accelerator utilisation, data centres can deliver more useful computing output from the same power capacity, potentially supporting greater economic value without a proportional increase in electricity demand.

## Make large loads smarter

Singapore’s demand-response and interruptible-load capacity grew from 71 MW in 2022 to 192 MW by June 2025. Under these programmes, participating large power users can temporarily reduce electricity demand when the system needs support, easing strain on the grid.

Data centres could contribute further, but expectations should be realistic. AI accelerators, including expensive graphics processing units used for AI computing, cannot simply be switched off whenever electricity demand peaks.

More practical opportunities may lie in batteries, uninterruptible power supplies, cooling systems and deprioritising tasks.

For instance, Google has shifted non-urgent data-centre computing to times when the grid is stressed. Microsoft has demonstrated how backup batteries at its Dublin data centre can support grid stability.

In Singapore, SP Group uses thermal storage in Marina Bay to reduce cooling-related electricity demand during peaks.

Notably, such measures must preserve critical services.

A data centre that can briefly reduce grid demand, draw on stored energy, or shift suitable workloads can provide flexibility without compromising critical services. The goal is not to turn data centres into power stations, but to make better use of their existing assets and controllable loads.

## Test before scaling

But theoretical discussions do not necessarily translate into real-life results. Component performance is not system performance.

Liquid-cooling systems, batteries and power converters may perform well in a laboratory, but may behave differently when combined with real processors, pumps, controls and tropical heat rejection.

That is why live test beds and brownfield demonstrations matter. The Sustainable Tropical Data Centre Testbed at the National University of Singapore allows cooling, power and control technologies to be evaluated as integrated systems under real operating conditions.

Such testing is especially relevant to Singapore and neighbouring South-east Asian markets, where high temperatures and humidity complicate cooling and energy efficiency.

Lessons from tropical test beds can help operators evaluate what works locally before committing to costly infrastructure upgrades.

Standards tell us what good performance should look like. Test beds show whether it can be delivered before expensive infrastructure choices are locked in.

## Raise the better question

Asking if Singapore can generate enough electricity for AI is too narrow.

The better question is whether every additional megawatt used by AI can create sufficient economic and strategic value while preserving reliability, affordability, resilience and Singapore’s path to net zero.

If Singapore can co-design power and compute, plan generation alongside demand, and devise computing, cooling and control systems together, AI need not simply become another load that the energy system must chase.

It can instead become a catalyst for a more resilient, efficient and intelligent energy system.

**The writer is head of the department of mechanical engineering, coordinating director of the NUS Energy Solutions Hub, and co-director of the NUS Sustainable Futures, National University of Singapore.**

stories.content:
This signals Nvidia’s continued support for neoclouds, a group of debt-laden AI cloud providers

\[SAN FRANCISCO\] Nvidia is in discussions to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in Firmus Grid after the Australian artificial intelligence cloud company abandoned an initial public offering, The Information reported.

The move signals that Nvidia will continue supporting neoclouds, a beleaguered group of debt-laden AI cloud providers, the news site said, citing unidentified people familiar with the talks.

Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, is already an investor in Firmus and a number of its peers.

A spokesperson for Santa Clara, California-based Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The report follows Firmus’ move earlier in October to scrap an IPO that would have been one of Australia’s biggest ever.

The company struggled to lure global investors, who have grown more wary of AI companies. Bloomberg News previously reported that Firmus was considering other funding options. BLOOMBERG

stories.summary: Jati Tinggi Group Bhd (KL:JTGROUP) on Wednesday reported a more than two-fold increase in quarterly net profit from a year earlier, driven by higher revenue from power infrastructure and underground cable projects, particularly those linked to data centres.

stories.title_zh: Jati Tinggi第三季度净利润翻倍以上，因数据中心项目贡献增强
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 28): Jati Tinggi Group Bhd (KL:JTGROUP) on Wednesday reported a more than two-fold increase in quarterly net profit from a year earlier, driven by higher revenue from power infrastructure and underground cable projects, particularly those linked to data centres.

Net profit for the third financial quarter ended Aug 31, 2026 (3QFY2026) rose to RM8.01 million from RM3.18 million, while revenue nearly tripled to RM156.05 million from RM52.96 million, according to the group's filing with Bursa Malaysia.

Jati Tinggi attributed the stronger performance to higher contributions from its substation engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning (EPCC) business, as well as underground utilities engineering services.

Major revenue contributors included a 275kV bulk power supply connection for a data centre in Johor, underground cable relocation works at Bandar Sri Pinang, and power infrastructure projects in Cyberjaya and Pasir Gudang.

On a quarter-on-quarter basis, revenue jumped 77.74% from RM87.8 million in 2QFY2026, mainly due to increased project activities and progress.

However, net profit declined from RM9.85 million in the preceding quarter as the group undertook more projects with lower profit margins. The previous quarter also benefitted from a RM2.31 million gain arising from its acquisition of a controlling stake in Roflex Pipe Sdn Bhd.

No dividend was declared for the quarter.

For the first nine months of FY2026, net profit more than tripled to RM18.96 million from RM5.86 million, while revenue surged to RM318.29 million from RM110.15 million.

Looking ahead, Jati Tinggi said it remains optimistic about its prospects, supported by continued demand for power infrastructure and data centre-related projects.

The group secured RM907.13 million worth of projects, including joint venture contracts, between December 2025 and Oct 22, 2026.

Its outstanding order book stood at RM1.4 billion as at Oct 22, providing earnings visibility for the next two to three financial years, said Jati Tinggi.

Among its recent wins was a RM30.1 million contract secured earlier this month to build power infrastructure for a data centre in Kulai, Johor.

Separately, Jati Tinggi said its wholly owned subsidiary, Jati Tinggi Holding Sdn Bhd, received two additional letters of award worth RM2.25 million from Public Bank Bhd (KL:PBBANK) for solar panel installation works, bringing the total contract value awarded under the project to RM10.06 million.

Jati Tinggi shares closed one sen or 0.78% higher at RM1.29 on Wednesday, valuing the group at RM571.4 million.

stories.title: Microsoft signs two PPAs with Macquarie-backed Blueleaf Energy in Japan
stories.summary: Blueleaf has a portfolio of around 1.2GW of solar projects in the Japanese market
stories.title_zh: Microsoft与麦格理支持的Blueleaf Energy在日本签署两份购电协议
stories.content:
Microsoft has signed two solar Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) in Japan with Macquarie Asset Management's portfolio company, Blueleaf Energy.

Details on the PPA are sparse, and the companies have not disclosed the capacity, contract length, or location of the solar farms. *DCD* has reached out for further information.

Under the terms of the agreements, which were coordinated by Macquarie’s Energy Markets and Customer Solutions team, Microsoft will act as the sole offtaker for the projects. The undisclosed projects are currently entering construction under a build-own-operate model, scheduled to start commercial operations in mid-2027.

Ed Northam, global head of MAM Green Investments, said: “These agreements reflect a relationship that has grown through successful collaboration across multiple markets. We are pleased to work with Microsoft again, supporting its business goals through tailored clean energy solutions that help meet growing global demand for cost-efficient, low-carbon power that can be delivered quickly.”

“Our collaboration with Microsoft is more than a commercial agreement; it is a shared blueprint for a decarbonized future. By bridging the energy landscapes of Japan and India, we are setting a new benchmark for how regional expertise and collaboration can accelerate the delivery of much-needed new generation capacity. These new PPAs in Japan stem from a trust built on the foundation of our successful delivery of the Pachora Hybrid Power Project in India,” added Raghuram Natarajan, CEO of Blueleaf Energy.

Blueleaf Energy is a major player in the Japanese solar market with a portfolio of almost 1.2GW of projects in various stages of deployment. According to the company, many of the projects include battery energy storage.

The deals build on an already existing relationship between Macquarie and Microsoft, with the companies working together since 2020. According to Macquarie, it has 540MW of capacity tied to power purchase agreements with Microsoft across the UK, Spain, and India.

The PPAs follow a major investment pledge by Microsoft into the Japanese market earlier this year. In April, the hyperscaler pledged a $10 billion investment in AI and cloud capabilities in Japan through the end of 2029.

Microsoft opened its Japanese data centers in 2014. Japan East is located in the Saitama Prefecture near Tokyo, while Japan West is in the Osaka Prefecture. The cloud giant has also previously signed PPAs with Shizen Energy in the country in 2023 and 2025.

stories.title: Nxera Singapore signs MoU with Sembcorp for supply of low carbon power in Singapore
stories.summary: Potential power solutions include hydrogen, biomethane, vertical solar, and floating solar
stories.title_zh: Nxera Singapore与Sembcorp签署谅解备忘录，为新加坡供应低碳电力
stories.content:
APAC data center developer Nxera Singapore has tapped Singaporean energy firm Sembcorp to supply renewable, low-carbon energy to power its data centers in the city-state.

The companies inked a non-binding Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to explore potential power solutions, which include low-carbon hydrogen-based generation, biomethane-based power generation, vertical building-applied photovoltaics, and renewable energy imports from the 2.2GW floating solar project at Linggiu Reservoir in Johor, Malaysia.

Commenting on the agreement, Koh Chiap Khiong, president & CEO, Gas and Related Services and CEO of Singapore, Sembcorp, said: “As AI adoption accelerates globally, demand for reliable, scalable and lower-carbon energy continues to grow. With a proven track record of powering the data center sector, Sembcorp is well-positioned to support this growth through our diversified energy portfolio. Our partnership with Nxera further affirms our shared ambition to enable the next generation of digital infrastructure while advancing the global energy transition.”

Bill Chang, CEO of Nxera and Singtel’s Digital InfraCo unit, added: “Working with Sembcorp gives us more options to power our growth sustainably and responsibly. Strengthening our energy resilience will be critical to underpinning Nxera’s long-term development in Singapore while supporting Singapore’s digital ambitions.”

Nxera Singapore is the AI data center arm of Singtel Group. Singtel is closing a number of small legacy data centers in Singapore, but still operates several large facilities in the city-state through the unit. Earlier this year, the company opened its 58MW DC Tuas data center in Singapore, its largest facility in Singapore at 58MW. The addition of the data center brought the company’s total capacity in the country to 120MW.

Nxera is also developing several facilities around Southeast Asia in partnership with local players and expects to grow its total capacity from 200MW to 400MW in the coming years. With more facilities in Batam and Johor due online in the second half of 2026, Nxera’s operational and pipeline capacity is expected to more than double from 200MW in 2026.

Sembcorp has signed several power agreements with data center providers over recent years. In March, the company signed a 25-year energy supply agreement with a subsidiary of Meta, Malkoha Pte, to construct, own, and operate a 150MW floating solar project in Singapore.

It eyes advanced manufacturing, high-tech industries, digital infrastructure sectors in Singapore, US and Japan

\[SINGAPORE\] Mapletree Industrial Trust (MIT) is looking beyond data centres for growth as it continues to divest older North American assets, pivot from a legacy-heavy portfolio and manage rising financing costs.

The CEO of the manager, Anand Tze Ming Chandran, who took on the role on Oct 1, said that the execution of North American divestments was the trust’s top business priority.

“I want the business to increase the diversification out of the data centre industrial vertical. That’s not to say we diminish it,” said Chandran, who was speaking at MIT’s second-quarter results briefing on Wednesday (Oct 28).

Previously the head of Mapletree Investments’ data centre division for the Asia-Pacific, he was tapped for the CEO position after Lily Ler left it to become Mapletree Investments’ chief financial officer.

In April, MIT announced plans that it would take one to two years to divest US$500 million to US$600 million in North American assets.

In August, it put a portfolio of 22 older US data centres up for sale, valued in aggregate at about US$1.24 billion, with US$1.07 billion attributable to the trust.

It is targeting to complete “a good amount” of the divestments by the end of its financial year on Mar 31, 2027, and is in talks with “a handful of parties” involving various parts of its portfolio, Chandran noted.

“If we have to take clear-eyed decisions about executing to get certainty, we will do it because a lot of portfolio pivot performance depends on the execution of the divestment.

“It will speak to everything to do, not just with income replacement and acquisitions, it will speak to our ability to manage shelter from (the) high-interest rate environment.

“It will speak to our ability to manage the hedge profile in a more optimal way. So that remains the top business priority, certainly between now and the end of the FY,” he said.

MIT will continue exploring opportunities in Singapore, the US and Japan, in sectors supported by advanced manufacturing, high-tech industries and digital infrastructure.

Asked how investors should view data centres’ contributions to MIT’s assets under management, relative to that by the general industrial sector, Chandran replied: “We will remain a general industrial Reit (real estate investment trust) with the ability to go down deep into specific verticals where we have strong conviction, as we have evidenced over the last five or so years in the data centre space.”

Data centres now account for 57.1 per cent or S$4.7 billion of MIT’s S$8.3 billion portfolio of assets under management.

Chandran said that the trust would seek to build relationships with a broader range of industrial tenants, adding that “any business needs to have strategic diversification”, whether across geographies or sectors.

He acknowledged that MIT’s footprint across primary and secondary North American data centre markets had “presented a challenge in recent years”.

“While we entered the market through acquisition as opposed to development, we have had to deal with the natural issues that come with the fast-changing market cycle in the US,” explained Chandran, adding: “I do not think it’s the right decision, strategically, to give up”.

He said that the trust would “work through the difficulties”.

For the quarter ended Sep 30, distribution per unit fell 6.6 per cent year on year to S$0.0297.

Q2 net property income declined 3.5 per cent to S$119.8 million, largely from lower contributions from North America, the absence of income from three Singapore industrial properties sold in August 2025, and depreciation of the Japanese yen against the Singapore dollar.

Portfolio occupancy slipped to 89.7 per cent from 90.7 per cent in the preceding quarter.

Data centre occupancy fell to 82.1 per cent from 85 per cent, while North American occupancy declined to 79.1 per cent from 82.5 per cent, when a lease on a San Diego property was not renewed in May.

When the news broke that MIT had put US$1 billion worth of its US assets up for sale in August, DBS analysts described the move as “surgical and decisive”, suggestive of a broader strategic review underway.

The bank’s Derek Tan wrote in an Aug 31 note: “In our view, this demonstrates greater urgency and decisiveness in addressing portfolio quality while sharpening MIT’s exposure to modern facilities, positioned to benefit from cloud and AI demand.”

The bank estimated that divesting 30 to 100 per cent of the marketed portfolio and applying all proceeds towards debt repayment could lower aggregate leverage to between 23.6 and 33.9 per cent, from 37.5 per cent.

“This would provide MIT with substantial capacity to pursue modern data-centre acquisitions and other high-specification facilities without requiring near-term equity fundraising,” the DBS report said.

In Singapore, MIT achieved a positive weighted average rental reversion rate of 6.9 per cent, up from 5.3 per cent in the preceding quarter, after 184 lease renewals covering about 640,000 square feet.

The management expects rental reversions to remain in the mid-single digits in the second half of the financial year.

Committed occupancy at Mapletree Hi-Tech Park @ Kallang Way, stands at 72.4 per cent. The property, completed in March 2023 in the trust’s largest redevelopment project, is expected to top 75 per cent occupancy by the financial year-end.

stories.title: Malaysia's utility pledges to connect data centers to the grid within one year: Report
stories.summary: Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB), Malaysia's national electricity utility, has committed to a one-year grid connection timeline for approved data center projects, according to chief distribution network officer Ahmad Sazree Abd Aziz. The pledge comes as Malaysia experiences surging demand from hyperscale and cloud operators expanding in the country.

stories.content:
Malaysia’s electricity utility, Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB) pledges to connect data centers to the grid within one year after approval by the relevant authority, Bernama reports quoting the utility’s chief distribution network officer Ahmad Sazree Abd Aziz.

“… once it’s been approved by the ministry-chaired committee, we pledge to get data centers connected to the grid in one year’s time,” he said at an event in Singapore yesterday.

The commitment is dependent on three measures that TNB is pursuing to accommodate exponential demand from energy-hungry data centers; namely demand forecasting, network capacity planning and targeted infrastructure development. Ahmad emphasized that strong domestic transmission and distribution networks were crucial to ensuring that Malaysia could fully benefit from the Asean Power Grid (APG). The regional grid aims to strengthen regional electricity security, but, this can only come about if the domestic network especially transmission and distribution is strong enough.

TNB is also ensuring that its networks were modernised and digitalised to facilitate renewable energy interconnections at the distribution level.

stories.summary: States without sufficient water supply will not be allowed to host data centres, even if land is available, as Malaysia tightens its approval process for new projects, Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said.

stories.title_zh: Johari Ghani表示，供水不足的州不允许建设数据中心
stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 28): States without sufficient water supply will not be allowed to host data centres, even if land is available, as Malaysia tightens its approval process for new projects, Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said.

Malaysia has no plans to impose a blanket moratorium on new data centres but will assess applications based on water availability, electricity supply and investors’ financial strength before granting approval.

Johari told the Dewan Rakyat during the winding-up debate on Budget 2027 on Wednesday that the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida) will work with state governments to assess water requirements, while electricity availability will be evaluated in consultation with Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA).

The government has approved 117 data centres nationwide, of which 55 are operational, 19 are under construction and 16 have received approval but have yet to begin construction. The remaining 27 are at various stages of development, with their electricity needs expected to be met through off-grid arrangements.

To protect Tenaga Nasional’s reserve margin and ensure sufficient electricity for other industries, the government has separated data centres’ electricity requirements from those of other industrial users.

Data centres supplied with electricity through Tenaga Nasional will be charged market rates without subsidies, Johari said. Operators must also pay for their contracted electricity capacity even if their actual consumption is lower.

For example, an operator that contracts for 300 megawatts (MW) but uses only 100MW must still pay for the remaining 200MW.

Data centre operators will also be required to meet a minimum local content requirement of 30% for data centre-related development.

Johari said the measures aim to ensure that data centre investments benefit Malaysia while taking into account the country’s water and electricity resources.

stories.summary: DE-CIX and IGC are establishing a new internet exchange in Bangkok, scheduled to launch in 2027 with connectivity to ASEAN regional hubs. The exchange will enable Thai networks to peer directly rather than routing traffic through Singapore or Hong Kong.

stories.content:
DE-CIX and International Gateway Co have formed a joint venture to launch DE-CIX Bangkok, an internet exchange due to be ready for service in 2027.

The venture will establish DE-CIX Thailand in Bangkok, building and operating the exchange as part of DE-CIX's Southeast Asian network.

The project will be the first internet exchange in Thailand to be directly interconnected with DE-CIX exchanges elsewhere in the ASEAN region. Networks connected in Bangkok will be able to peer directly with networks in Singapore, Johor Bahru, Kuala Lumpur, Penang and Jakarta through a single regional platform.

The launch will extend DE-CIX's Southeast Asian platform to a seventh metropolitan market. The countries of mainland Southeast Asia - Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar - account for about half of all end users in the ASEAN region, according to the operator.

IGC will provide connectivity to the Bangkok exchange and act as a reseller for customers across mainland Southeast Asia. The exchange will also connect to DE-CIX's global backbone, linking more than 4,600 networks across the Americas, Africa, Europe, the Middle East and Asia.

### Regional reach

Bangkok is one of Southeast Asia's faster-growing digital infrastructure markets, with submarine connectivity into the Pacific and Indian Oceans and a growing data centre sector. Its location also makes it a gateway to mainland Southeast Asia, DE-CIX said.

DE-CIX already operates exchanges in Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia through its distributed ASEAN platform. Close to 150 networks are connected, or in the process of connecting, across that regional interconnection fabric, it said.

"Thailand is the next logical step in our Southeast Asian growth strategy," said Ivo Ivanov, Chief Executive Officer of DE-CIX. "The country has all the ingredients to become the gateway to mainland Southeast Asia and one of the region's leading digital connectivity hubs, serving millions of people. Together with IGC, we are creating an environment where networks in Thailand can interconnect locally while gaining seamless access to one of Southeast Asia's richest digital ecosystems. Customers will benefit from lower latency, greater resilience, and direct access to cloud, AI, content, and network providers across the DE-CIX platform."

DE-CIX operates internet exchanges in 60 locations worldwide and says its services are accessible from data centres in more than 600 cities. Founded in 1995, it is one of the largest operators in the sector, with DE-CIX Frankfurt alone handling more than 48 exabytes of data traffic a year as of 2025.

IGC, a subsidiary of ALT Telecom, provides wholesale bandwidth, IP transit and network services for domestic and international traffic in Thailand. It operates more than 12,000 kilometres of optical fibre nationwide and has network-to-network interfaces across 12 active border crossings, linking 42 operators in neighbouring countries and Thailand.

Its infrastructure also includes connectivity to more than 10 data centres in Thailand and licences covering five cable landing stations. DE-CIX plans to use that domestic and cross-border footprint to extend access to the new exchange beyond Bangkok.

"The establishment of DE-CIX Bangkok will create new opportunities for customers to exchange traffic not only locally but regionally, while reducing latency, improving network performance, and providing access to one of the most interconnected ecosystems in Southeast Asia," said Supat Eamwiwat, Chief Executive Officer of IGC. "We are excited to partner with DE-CIX to support the next phase of Thailand's digital growth."

stories.title: Thailand drafts new data center governance law
stories.summary: Thailand's Data Center Policy Committee has approved a draft law for data center governance. This framework aims to regulate investment and operations for sustainable digital economy development.
stories.content:
Thailand's Data Center Policy Committee has approved a draft policy for data center governance, according to local reports. The draft, reportedly scheduled for Cabinet consideration on 3 November 2026, establishes a regulatory framework for investment and operation of data centers.The policy defines a data center as a building with electronic equipment providing data services to non-affiliated companies, requiring a minimum electricity demand of 0.5 megawatts (MW).
### Key Policy Directives

A one-stop center will be established to coordinate approvals and licensing through the TH-DC Dashboard system. This system will consolidate processes from various government agencies.The draft also proposes four minimum standards for operators. These cover location and land use, utility network connections, environmental standards, and economic and social contributions.Data centers will be classified into seven levels based on power demand, ranging from Level 1 (0–0.5 MW) to Level 7 (200 MW and above). Each level will have different requirements.New laws or amendments are expected to take approximately 8–12 months for enforcement of these minimum standards. Guidelines for a transition period have also been established.These guidelines apply to data centers already in operation, those with construction permits before August 11, 2026, and those with permits from August 11, 2026, onwards. Projects expanding power capacity by over 20MW will consider the expanded portion a new project.The policy aims to promote Green Data Centers. This supports the country's goal of net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, alongside other sustainability objectives.

stories.summary_zh: 由 Nvidia 支持的印尼 AI 基础设施平台 Zankore 正在银团分销一笔 31 亿美元的贷款，用于 GPU 采购。该交易代表了新兴亚洲地区最大的 AI 基础设施债务融资之一。

stories.content:
(Oct 28): Zankore, an Indonesian artificial intelligence infrastructure platform backed by Nvidia Corp, is syndicating a US$3.1 billion (RM12.65 billion) loan to the broader market, according to people familiar with the matter, adding to a flurry of financing for Asia’s AI buildout.

The five-year loan, which funds the purchase of graphics processing units for Zankore’s new AI factory, will pay an interest margin of 330 basis points over the Secured Overnight Financing Rate, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters. United Overseas Bank Ltd and Citigroup Inc are among the five original underwriters marketing the deal, with other banks invited to join in the senior phase as underwriters or bookrunners, the people said.

Citigroup and UOB declined to comment while Zankore did not respond to requests for comment.

The deal adds to a wave of debt financing backing Asia’s AI infrastructure boom, as regional lenders increasingly look beyond data centre construction to financing GPUs. Moody’s Ratings expects at least US$3 trillion in data centre-related investment over the next five years, even as investors scrutinise lofty AI valuations.

Blackstone-owned AirTrunk secured a A$4.25 billion (RM12.19 billion) green loan for a Sydney data centre campus while Blue Owl Capital-owned Stack Infrastructure Inc is seeking a A$8.6 billion facility for a buildout in Melbourne.

Zankore’s financing is supported by a six-year contract with Nvidia that includes revenue sharing and credit support, helping reduce lenders’ repayment risk, the people said. The arrangement applies to any unsold compute capacity from an initial 100MW, they said.

US fintech companies are the offtakers, buying GPU compute capacity from Zankore, the people added.

stories.summary: CoreWeave, an American cloud computing company, has marked its first deployment in Denmark by partnering with atNorth, a Nordic data center company, to host 22.5 MW IT capacity at the DEN01 data center in Copenhagen. According to a CoreWeave press release, the deployment is scheduled to come online in Q4 2026, with a full network […]
stories.content:
CoreWeave, an American cloud computing company, has marked its first deployment in Denmark by partnering with atNorth, a Nordic data center company, to host 22.5 MW IT capacity at the DEN01 data center in Copenhagen.

According to a CoreWeave press release, the deployment is scheduled to come online in Q4 2026, with a full network loop expected by mid 2027. The facility uses NVIDIA Blackwell systems connected through NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand technology. CoreWeave also agreed to supply surplus heat to Copenhagen’s district heating network.

“Modern workloads demand digital infrastructure that is not only high performance, but also energy efficient and responsibly operated,” said Eyjólfur Magnús Kristinsson, CEO, atNorth. “By partnering with atNorth, CoreWeave gains access to DEN01’s infrastructure, designed for GPU-intensive processing, while supporting renewable energy development through power purchase agreements and helping warm local homes through heat reuse, contributing to the green transition.”

The Denmark deployment brings CoreWeave’s European footprint to nine data centers across five countries which are Denmark, United Kingdom, Spain, Sweden and Norway. The company is also expanding its global AI network into the Middle East and Asia Pacific, adding network points of presence in the United Arab Emirates, India, Indonesia, Singapore, Australia, South Korea and Japan.

“Our customers need more than access to computing capacity. They need infrastructure that performs reliably at scale and the ability to move data and workloads wherever their business requires,” said Sachin Jain, Chief Operating Officer, CoreWeave. “We’re expanding our global infrastructure and the network connecting it together, so customers can focus on building and improving AI rather than managing the complexity underneath it.”

The expansion will extend Corweave’s existing network across North America and Europe into four continents. Each location uses multiple 400-gigabit-per-second connections, hardware-based MACsec encryption and redundant network paths to support secure, high-volume data transfers between regions.

Since June 30, 2026, CoreWeave operated 51 data centers worldwide with more than 1.5 GW of active power capacity and reported approximately 4.2 GW of contracted power during its August 11, 2026, earnings call.

KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 28): The Energy Commission is developing a comprehensive framework and guidelines on self-generation facilities and the use of renewable energy for the data centre sector, said Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Fadillah Yusof.

He said the initiative is in line with the government’s decision to require the sector to use at least 30% renewable energy.

He said the data centre industry was also encouraged to develop self-generation facilities through solar initiatives for its own consumption, to prevent an increase in electricity supply costs for other consumers.

“This approach aims to increase the use of self-generated energy by the data centre sector while reducing its full dependence on electricity supplied by the national grid.

“In addition, data centres need to be equipped with backup generators that can be utilised for demand control, particularly to reduce additional pressure on the grid system during critical periods and when operating reserves are low,” he said during the question-and-answer session in the Dewan Rakyat on Wednesday.

He was responding to a question from Wan Ahmad Fayhsal Wan Ahmad Kamal (PN-Machang) on the government’s contingency plan to ensure that data centre operations do not affect the people’s electricity and water supply during droughts or supply disruptions.

Fadillah said data centres were also encouraged to participate in the Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme to obtain green energy supply directly.

He said every application for electricity supply for data centre development undergoes a comprehensive technical assessment by the Energy Focus Group before being brought to the Data Centre Task Force, taking into account the system’s capacity to supply electricity, the electricity transmission and distribution network, as well as infrastructure investment requirements.

Fadillah said that as of August 2026, contracted electricity demand from data centres stood at 2,346 megawatts (MW), while actual consumption was 1,374 MW, or 58.5%.

He said this was because the estimated electricity requirements submitted when applying for supply contracts did not necessarily correspond to actual consumption.

In response to a supplementary question from Wan Ahmad Fayhsal on the use of nuclear energy, Fadillah said the government was still considering its use as one of the country’s energy sources, with national preparedness as the priority to ensure energy supply and public safety.

He said matters relating to international agreements needed to be resolved first, in addition to ensuring compliance with the standards of the International Atomic Energy Agency, safety regulatory requirements, workforce capacity and technological suitability.

stories.summary: Australian Energy Minister Chris Bowen has directed the AEMC to evaluate a rule change that would impose a firmed energy obligation on qualifying data centers, requiring them to match consumption with reliable, dispatchable power rather than intermittent renewables alone. stories.content:
Australia’s energy minister Chris Bowen has asked the Australian Energy Market Commission (AEMC) to consider a rule change. This proposal would require qualifying data centres to back their electricity consumption with firmed energy.The government seeks to limit the impact of rapidly growing digital infrastructure demand on power prices and grid reliability. The rule change request, received by the AEMC on 20 October, proposes mandatory contracting arrangements. These would be supported by new generation, storage and dependable demand flexibility in the same electricity market region as each data centre.
### Addressing growing demand

Data centre consumption is forecast to reach around 15 TWh annually by 2029-30, representing 7.8 per cent of operational electricity consumption in the National Electricity Market (NEM). By 2035-36, consumption is projected to reach approximately 34 TWh, or 13 per cent. The government argues that data centre demand could grow faster than new generation, storage and network capacity can be delivered. This is particularly relevant as coal-fired power stations retire and variable renewable generation takes a greater share of the electricity mix.Under the proposed obligation, data centres would need to demonstrate that their contracting portfolios provide sufficient firm capacity. This capacity must match the timing, duration and scale of their electricity demand. Potentially eligible arrangements include power purchase agreements, cap contracts, tolling agreements, storage and dependable demand response. A central element of the proposal is a requirement for supporting capacity to come from new investment.
### Compliance and coordination

The Australian Energy Regulator (AER) could assess a data centre’s full 24-hour demand profile rather than focusing solely on peak periods. Compliance could be assessed before a facility connects to the grid and at scheduled reviews or following material increases in demand. Financial penalties are proposed for non-compliance. The AEMC is also asked to consider whether facilities could be required to reduce their electricity consumption until they meet their obligations.The proposal builds on advice from the AEMC, which informed a reform package energy ministers agreed on 28 July. This request was lodged alongside a second rule change request on connection agreements for large energy users. The contracting obligation will need to be coordinated with the government’s renewable electricity obligation for data centres. The request identifies the risk of duplicated requirements, administrative burden and additional costs if the two frameworks are not aligned. No final requirements or implementation timetable have been set.

stories.content:
The specialist GPU cloud market is set for significant consolidation, with Gartner predicting that more than 80 per cent of neocloud providers will cease independent operations by 2030.Neoclouds are cloud providers built specifically to rent out GPU capacity for artificial intelligence (AI) training and inference. The field is expected to shrink through mergers, acquisitions, and failures, driven primarily by capital constraints.Providers fund GPU purchases largely with debt, and servicing this debt is becoming more expensive. CoreWeave, a Nasdaq-listed neocloud, reported net interest expenses of approximately $640 million in Q2 2026, up from $267 million a year earlier, and ended the quarter with roughly $35 billion of debt.Investor concern intensified in October following several key developments. On 14 October, Gartner warned that over $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could face impairment by the end of 2030 if current capital expenditure continues.The Information reported on 18 October that industry executives anticipate only seven to 10 neoclouds will survive. On 25 October, Elon Musk noted that debt markets had "almost entirely shut off" funding for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centres.Depreciation of rapidly acquired assets further adds to the financial pressure, with Gartner stating that failing to earn a sustainable return would likely force write-downs. Nvidia's role is expected to be decisive, as it backs several neoclouds including CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN, and Lambda, and has begun guaranteeing utilisation floors for some partners.Consolidation does not mean the infrastructure disappears; GPUs, power contracts, and sites are more likely to change hands. However, delivery risk is rising, as exemplified by Microsoft withdrawing as an anchor tenant at Nscale’s Loughton site due to grid delays pushing power into the 2030s.For data centre landlords, counterparty strength is becoming paramount, while enterprise buyers must scrutinise providers' balance sheets, debt levels, and exit terms alongside GPU pricing.

stories.title: Asia Pacific construction costs set to outpace Europe
stories.summary: Developers face higher budgets as JLL sees Asia Pacific tender inflation at 3.8% to 4.7% in 2027, above Europe's forecast.
stories.title_zh: 亚太地区建设成本预计将超过欧洲
stories.content:
Wed, 28th Oct 2026 (Today)
JLL has forecast construction tender price inflation in Asia Pacific of 3.8% to 4.7% in 2027, with the region likely to outpace Europe on construction cost growth.

The forecast, in JLL's Global Construction Costs Index 2026, points to continued pressure on developers, investors and occupiers across Asia Pacific. The report cites a mix of geopolitical disruption to energy and material supply chains, labour shortages, and land scarcity in major urban markets.

Asia Pacific's expected inflation range for 2027 compares with 3.2% to 4.2% in North America and 2.2% to 3.5% in Europe, placing the region alongside North America and ahead of Europe as construction budgets remain under strain.

One of the main factors is the effect of conflict in the Middle East on input costs in Asia Pacific. The region's dependence on Middle Eastern energy supplies and construction materials, combined with more complex logistics routes, has left it exposed to higher freight costs and delays.

Energy-intensive materials including steel, aluminium and cement have seen sustained price increases across Asia Pacific markets, with those rises flowing through to project budgets as contractors adjust pricing for disruption and uncertainty.

"A variety of factors, most noticeably geopolitical impact, is ensuring Asia Pacific developers are navigating an extremely challenging cost environment into 2027," said Matt Bennion, Head of Project and Development Services, Asia Pacific, JLL.

"The combination of supply chain vulnerability, structural labor constraints, and intense AI-driven demand for technical facilities has created cost pressures that exceed what we're seeing in Western markets. Postponing projects in hopes of relief is no longer viable; organizations must transition to a more agile approach to risk management and engagement of supply chains to maintain project viability," Bennion said.

### Inflation gap

JLL also pointed to a widening gap between consumer inflation and building cost inflation in several major Asia Pacific economies. In Australia, construction costs have risen about 1.5 times as fast as the consumer price index since 2021, while in Singapore and Japan, construction inflation has run 1.5 to 2 times ahead of broader inflation measures.

That divergence matters for project underwriting because developers often use consumer inflation as a benchmark for cost escalation. The report warns that this approach risks understating actual build costs and can force projects to be reassessed during delivery.

Labour costs are another source of pressure. Construction wages rose between 8% and 35% across key Asia Pacific markets between 2020 and 2026, outpacing both consumer inflation and material cost growth.

JLL linked those increases to demographic changes, limited trade training capacity, and competition for skilled workers from data centres and advanced manufacturing. Those factors are creating a higher baseline for labour costs rather than a short-term spike.

"Energy price volatility, transportation disruption and base materials costs all feed directly into regional tender prices. Increasingly, contractors are now pricing in geopolitical uncertainty as a permanent risk premium rather than a temporary measure," said Shweta Choudhari, Director, Work Dynamics Research, Asia Pacific, JLL.

"Our construction inflation forecast of between 3.8% to 4.7% reinforces compounding factors that both developers and investors are explicitly planning for," Choudhari said.

### Urban premiums

The report highlighted Hong Kong and Singapore as two markets where land constraints are driving construction costs well above regional benchmarks, particularly for industrial and logistics projects. Global averages for that asset class typically range from USD $1,010 to USD $1,560 per square metre.

In Hong Kong, industrial and logistics construction costs now approach or exceed USD $2,500 per square metre. In Singapore, the high end of the range is about USD $1,750 per square metre.

Those figures reflect land scarcity, complex site conditions, vertical development requirements and regulatory demands. The higher cost structure is also influencing capital allocation, as some developers weigh alternatives in other regional markets or assess cross-border logistics networks instead of concentrating spending in gateway cities.

The issue is especially notable because industrial and logistics assets are usually among the least expensive forms of commercial development. In Hong Kong and Singapore, however, that pattern has been reversed by urban constraints.

For investors and developers, the current market requires more frequent reviews of project feasibility and broader consideration of alternatives to ground-up construction. These include retrofits and repositioning of existing assets, especially where they offer lower costs or shorter delivery periods than new schemes.

"Construction costs across Asia Pacific have reset at a higher level than anywhere else globally, and owners should plan around that rather than wait for relief that isn't coming," Bennion said.

"The owners who keep delivering returns in Asia Pacific are the ones who test feasibility against live cost data from day one, re-confirm it at every design and procurement gate, and consider retrofit and repositioning where it can beat ground-up on cost, speed, and carbon," he added.

stories.title: Nvidia Vera Rubin and Vera CPUs now generally available on Oracle
stories.summary: And other AI hardware deployments soon to arrive
stories.title_zh: Nvidia Vera Rubin和Vera CPU现已在Oracle全面上市
stories.content:
The latest generation of Nvidia hardware is entering general availability on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.

Announced during the Oracle AI World event, the Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs are now generally available on Oracle’s cloud platform.

Oracle is also set to add the Nvidia Vera Rubin systems to its “Superclusters” offering, which will be a multi-gigawatt-scale deployment. At a later date, the Rubin HGX NVL8 Systems will also be added, which will offer eight Rubin GPUs connected through NVLink in an x86-based server configuration.

OCI Superclusters combine Nvidia NVL72 rack-scale systems, Oracle Acceleron networking with Nvidia Spectrum-X Ethernet networking featuring Nvidia Spectrum-6 switches and Nvidia BlueField-4 DPUs, and gigawatt-class power and cooling to train and serve the largest AI models. Each rack connects 72 GPUs through Nvidia NVLink scale-up networking, while OCI’s resilient, multiplanar network scales across hundreds of thousands of GPUs.

The addition of Vera Rubin to Superclusters builds on Oracle’s existing Nvidia Grace Blackwell compute that is available in the formation and was used in Abilene by OpenAI to train GPT-6 Astra.

OpenAI used an OCI Supercluster of more than 100,000 Blackwell GPUs.

“As our frontier models advance, we need infrastructure that can keep pace,” said Sreekanth Pothanis, engineering leader, compute infra at OpenAI. “Nvidia Vera Rubin on OCI gives us the computing performance and scale to accelerate model training and serve increasingly demanding AI workloads.”

The deployment of Vera CPUs alone is targeting agentic AI workloads, combining high single-thread performance with memory bandwidth to help agents complete CPU-intensive tasks faster.

“Oracle Cloud Infrastructure gives customers the performance, security and scale to advance frontier AI,” said Mahesh Thiagarajan, president of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Oracle. “Our collaboration with Nvidia extends those capabilities across training, inference and agentic AI. By combining Nvidia Vera Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs with Oracle Acceleron networking and AI-optimized data centers, we’re helping customers keep GPUs productive, secure, and scale efficiently as their needs grow.”

## Oracle goes CPU crazy

Beyond Nvidia hardware, Oracle has announced a multi-year collaboration with Intel to expand Intel Xeon-based computing on OCI, including current Xeon platforms and the planned OCI X14 offerings based on Intel’s next-generation server processor codenamed Diamond Rapids.

CPUs are becoming increasingly important to AI workloads as AI agents are being rapidly adopted. The partnership with Intel will increase CPU capacity on OCI, while giving customers access to familiar tooling and software environments.

“As AI agents scale, they need processors that can run software, move and secure data, and accelerate inference. Xeon brings together performance and hardware-based confidential computing, giving organizations a trusted, cost-effective foundation for AI at scale,” said Kevork Kechichian, executive vice president and general manager, Intel Data Center Group. “Our expanded collaboration with Oracle is intended to combine Intel's multigenerational roadmap with Oracle Cloud Infrastructure’s technology to help customers put AI to work faster and more cost-effectively.”

Planned Diamond Rapids-based OCI X14 offerings will target both AI and general-purpose computing, including Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) with FP8, FP16, and BF16 support for inference, and Intel Advanced Performance Extensions (APX) to help applications execute with less instruction overhead.

Meanwhile, with AMD, Oracle is nearing bringing online its E7 instances that will use sixth-generation AMD Epyc processors, with AMD Pensando DPUs supporting Oracle Acceleron NICs for AMD-powered instances.

The E7 instances are designed to support CPU work surrounding AI models. The instances use 6th Gen AMD Epyc processors from the Epyc 9006 Server Processor Series. 6th Gen Epyc processors provide up to 256 cores and 512 threads per socket, up to 1,024 MB of L3 cache, 16 memory channels with up to 8000 MTps, and PCIe 6.0 connectivity. These provide significant uplifts over 5th Gen Epyc CPUs, and the company says they power enterprise workloads more quickly and efficiently, and allow for the deployment of more agents per instance and per watt.

## Oracle to deploy Cerebras, SambaNova, and Positron

Oracle has further revealed plans to bring a variety of chip architectures onto its platform, including Cerebras’ wafer-scale compute, SambaNova’s chips, and more.

The Cerebras chips are designed for high-speed AI inference, and integrate compute and memory on a single wafer-scale processor to reduce data movement and inter-chip communication.

“People want AI that can do valuable work quickly,” said Andrew Feldman, co-founder and CEO of Cerebras. “Every step an agent makes requires inference, whether it’s reasoning, checking its work, or taking action. The faster the inference, the more work AI can do without making users wait. Bringing Cerebras fast inference to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure gives AI labs, enterprises, and developers the speed to build agents that do more, faster.”

Cerebras Inference on OCI is planned to be available in calendar year 2027.

Details about the SambaNova partnership remain sparse, beyond that Oracle will bring online the SN50 chip from the company. No specific timeline has yet been provided.

The final player is the Positron Atlas chip, which is now generally available on OCI.

Positron Atlas Inference Servers are purpose-built for Large Language Models, and deliver low-latency performance for popular open-weight models. Positron Atlas is networked through Oracle Acceleron.

Atlas is Positron's first-generation chip, was fabricated by Intel in the US, and is currently shipping to customers. Positron claims the hardware can achieve three times the compute-per-watt of Nvidia’s H100 GPUs and support up to 500-billion-parameter models.

The new chips coming to OCI join the Google TPU, which Oracle today revealed was set to be deployed on OCI under a multi-year and multi-gigawatt contract.

stories.title: Oracle will offer Google's TPU AI chips via OCI in multi-gigawatt deployment
stories.summary: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure will become the first non-Google hyperscaler to offer Google's Tensor Processing Unit chips, with plans for a multi-gigawatt deployment. The partnership represents a rare instance of competitive cloud providers collaborating on proprietary AI silicon rather than relying solely on in-house or Nvidia alternatives.
stories.why_it_matters: Oracle breaking the TPU exclusivity wall forces a recalculation of cloud AI strategies across the industry: customers gain bargaining power and architectural flexibility, Google monetizes its silicon investment beyond its own footprint, and Nvidia faces a credible alternative accelerator in a major rival's stack. The multi-gigawatt scale signals this is not a niche experiment but a structural challenge to GPU dominance in training workloads.

stories.summary_zh: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure将成为首个提供Google TPU chips的非Google hyperscaler，计划进行multi-gigawatt deployment。该合作代表了竞争性cloud providers在proprietary AI silicon上协作的罕见案例，而非仅依赖in-house或Nvidia替代方案。
stories.why_zh: Oracle打破TPU exclusivity wall迫使整个行业重新计算cloud AI战略：客户获得议价能力和架构灵活性，Google在其自身footprint之外实现silicon投资变现，Nvidia在主要竞争对手的stack中面临可信的alternative accelerator。Multi-gigawatt规模表明这不是一个niche experiment，而是对GPU在training workload中主导地位的结构性挑战。
stories.content:
Oracle and Google are partnering to enable Oracle to offer Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) from Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI).

Oracle will deploy the TPUs within its data center infrastructure, making it the first hyperscaler to adopt the chips since Google announced in April 2026 that it would be offering its chips for sale to a “select group of customers.”

“Different AI workloads have different compute needs,” said Mahesh Thiagarajan, president, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Oracle.

“Bringing Google TPUs to OCI gives customers access to multiple leading AI compute architectures in one cloud. That choice gives them the flexibility to choose the right infrastructure for the performance, throughput, and economics of each AI workload.”

Google is currently on its eighth generation of TPUs, having spent more than a decade developing the chips. The TPU 8t is designed for training and can deliver nearly 3x the compute performance per pod over the previous generation, while TPU 8i is an inference chip designed to handle the iterative work of many specialized agents.

TPU 8t has 19.2Tbps of bidirectional scale-up bandwidth and 400Gbps of scale-out networking bandwidth, with Google introducing a new networking architecture to support the hardware. Called Virgo Network, the company claims it supports a 4x increase in data center bandwidth and has been built on high-radix switches that reduce network layers.

Meanwhile, designed with more memory bandwidth to serve latency-sensitive inference workloads, the TPU 8i is scalable to 1,152 chips in a single pod. It delivers 11.6 exaflops of FP8 compute performance, with a total HBM capacity of 331.8TB per pod and 19.2Tbps of bidirectional scale-up bandwidth per chip.

## Oracle eyes gigawatts of TPUs

While Oracle declined to comment on the scale of the initial deployment, Karan Batta, SVP of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, told *DCD* at the Oracle AI World event in Las Vegas that it would be a “multi-year, multi-gigawatt partnership with Google and it will look and feel the same as it does from a GCP standpoint.”

He added: “What I can tell you is that this is not an experiment. This is going to be a cloud gigawatt-scale investment from Oracle over time, and the best way to think of it is that when Google launches a new TPU, we will have it on day one.”

Google TPUs on OCI will be available in calendar year 2027, ramping over a multi-year period to meet customer needs.

Google is also working with Blackstone to create a US-based cloud platform offering its TPUs, named Crux AI. Neocloud Fluidstack is also known to be deploying TPUs for Anthropic in a series of Google-backed deals. Depending on which launches sooner, Oracle could be the first to bring TPUs online outside Google's platform.
