stories.content:
Amazon has ended a six-year legal battle with two former AWS managers accused of taking kickbacks for certain data center deals.

Carl Nelson and Casey Kirschner, who were named in the 2020 lawsuit alongside Denver-based real estate firm Northstar Commercial Partners, said in a joint statement that they “regret their actions” and “apologize for failing to meet Amazon’s high ethical standards.”

They said that the payments broke Amazon’s code of conduct and put the company’s reputation at risk.

Nelson and Kirschner had been accused of engaging Northstar in nine different build-to-suit leasing projects for Amazon in Virginia worth hundreds of millions of dollars in exchange for kickbacks delivered as “referral fees” through a trust owned by Kirschner’s brother, Christian Kirschner.

According to court documents, the fees were calculated as a percentage of the fees Northstar received on its Amazon leases. During Northstar’s business with Amazon, more than $5 million went to the trust.

The trust then transferred money to Christian Kirschner and other entities that funneled funds to Nelson and Casey Kirschner.

Amazon said that its costs in these transactions were inflated to fund the kickbacks, with Northstar CEO Brian Watson baking fees into project budgets and inflating Amazon’s rent.

In a TikTok video, Nelson’s wife, Amy Nelson, said all disputes between Nelson and Amazon had been resolved. Terms of the settlement were not disclosed.

Over the years, the case saw several rulings both for and against Amazon. In 2023, a federal judge ruled that Amazon’s code of conduct wasn’t an enforceable contract, and dismissed most claims against Nelson and Kirschner.

But last year, the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit revived several claims and sent the case back to trial.

The case against Northstar will continue, with a trial date of November 2.

stories.title: Google data center hearing in Hermantown, Minnesota, shut down due to protests
stories.summary: Hearing pushed back a day, but project faces lawsuits and other challenges
stories.content:
A hearing for a proposed data center in Hermantown, Minnesota, was shut down amid protests.

The 1.66 million square foot (154,220 sqm) Google data center in Duluth was widely expected to be approved, but the meeting was adjourned after police stopped proceedings. The meeting has been moved to Tuesday, October 27, at 7.30pm.

The Hermantown City Council meeting saw both pro- and anti-data center groups converge, with the latter, larger 'Stop the Hermantown Data Center' movement loudly chanting anti-data center slogans.

The pro-data center group, mostly wearing green tops promoting the business lobby-backed 501(c)(4) Jobs for Minnesotans, sat quietly in the chamber halls. The 'Stop the' protesters were primarily outside the halls, but some managed to get in to make their voice heard.

Following two hours of delay over the loud protests, the meeting was adjourned, and Chief of Police Jim Crace told the crowd that they had ten minutes to leave or face detainment for an unsafe and unlawful gathering that disrupts civil process.

"Hermantown has always been a town where neighbors can disagree with respect," city councilor Andy Hjelle said in a statement.

"People care deeply about what happens here, and passionate discussion is part of small-town life. But shouting down a public meeting to the point where our police officers had to declare an unlawful assembly is completely wrong. That is not who we are, and it is not how Hermantown gets things done."

He added: "Tonight, local folks drove down to City Hall just wanting to take part in their local government. Instead, a coordinated disruption took over the room, shouted down normal business, and drowned out the voices of everyday residents."

Incumbent Hjelle faces a number of opponents in the four-candidate race for two seats on the Hermantown City Council. Data centers remain a key topic on the ballot box, with Hjelle claiming that they will help lower property taxes. He has proposed a data center dividend, which could generate $3 million annually in new city property taxes from the Google facility.

Opponents Emma Richtman, Miranda McKay-Chambers, and Candi Mock have all called for more community involvement and greater transparency, with Richtman a member of the Stop the Hermantown Data Center movement.

Ahead of the delayed vote, Google dropped a request for up to $80m in tax subsidies, reduced the size of the facility, added a well monitoring program, and committed to a quieter campus. The council was also set to vote on whether to approve an agreement with Google to pay to decommission the site if it ceases operations, a first for the hyperscaler.

Should the facility be approved in the latest attempt at a vote, the data center would still need to seek a federal air permit as well as certain state permits. The council has already voted in favor of Minnesota Power building transmission lines to the facility.

Eighty acres of the 234-acre site are also tied up in a lawsuit, as residents claim that they sold the land for a solar farm and were misled over its eventual end use. Another lawsuit claims that the data center project violates zoning restrictions.

stories.title: Sponsored: Ground control: Structuring land deals for data center development
stories.summary: AI and unprecedented demand for compute have fundamentally altered how investors, developers and operators evaluate opportunities
stories.content:
Historically, site selection was driven by proximity to customers, land availability, connectivity, and planning. Site selection now also involves data sovereignty, power, water and other infrastructure, environmental constraints, community acceptance, supply chain resilience and access to capital. Governments take a more active role in shaping digital infrastructure, and capital is entering earlier in the development lifecycle.

The result is a new location equation. Success now requires aligning infrastructure, regulation, customer demand, planning and environmental deliverability, social licence and capital. The most attractive sites are those where these factors are assembled into a deliverable, scalable development package.

## A new site selection framework

Site selection starts with the intended use. Edge and latency-sensitive applications still prioritise proximity to users, fibre networks and major exchanges. AI training clusters and sovereign compute platforms can tolerate greater distance from users in exchange for the infrastructure needed for high-density computing.

As AI becomes a strategic national priority, regulatory frameworks are becoming a key differentiator between markets, and planning now sits at the heart of location strategy. Some governments are accelerating deployment in selected areas through planning support, infrastructure funding and access to land. Others are tightening controls in response to environmental concerns, resource constraints and community opposition.

In some markets, accelerated deployment quickly gives way to tighter controls, driven largely by community opposition.

## Power remains the defining constraint

Power has emerged as the dominant constraint in many markets, followed by water supply and social opposition. Power is the gateway through which all other site-selection decisions are filtered: a location may satisfy customer, connectivity and commercial requirements but remain unviable if power cannot be delivered timely.

Investors globally prioritise locations where power infrastructure and planning strategy are aligned.

**Governments are actively shaping where and how digital infrastructure is deployed.**

**In Asia-Pacific**, governments are linking data center development to wider economic and sustainability objectives. Singapore uses structured programmes to allocate infrastructure capacity. Japan is deploying incentives to encourage development beyond Tokyo and Osaka. India has designated data centres as essential infrastructure, with states competing for investment through land and other incentives. In Australia, the focus on which projects can actually energise has driven regulatory reform, clean energy mandates, queue management initiatives and greater scrutiny of speculative projects.

**In the United States**, demand continues to outpace supply, pushing development beyond established clusters. Pressure on power, infrastructure and local communities is driving attention towards regions that offered greater capacity and planning certainty. But as demand escalates, regions are introducing measures to curb speculative projects, impose “bring your own generation” and emergency curtailment requirements, and audit water and land use by data centres, balancing rapid load growth against grid reliability and scarce natural resources.

**Europe** combines strong demand with increasingly sophisticated sustainability and reporting requirements, while development remains shaped by local planning controls, grid availability and environmental requirements. Spain’s draft rules illustrate the direction of travel: grid access for new data centres of 1 MW or more would be tied to resilience and digital sovereignty, energy and water efficiency, renewable power and disclosure requirements, with non-compliance risking loss of access permits.

**The UK** has designated data infrastructure as Critical National Infrastructure, emphasizing their importance to economic growth and digitalisation. The National Planning Policy Framework (August 2026) strengthens support for data centres and their locational requirements, including electricity network infrastructure. Newly designated AI Growth Zones offer selected sites streamlined planning and other incentives. Harder-edged legal reforms are speeding up consenting: data centres need not follow any prescribed consenting route, and new flexibility means planning strategy can bend to accommodate power strategy. Judicial review reforms aim to limit the ability of legal challenges to stall important projects.

**The Middle East** is increasingly encouraging data center development as part of broader digital economy and AI strategies. The UAE has risen to regional prominence by offering a stable environment for investment, significant tax incentives, and streamlined licensing procedures, underpinned by strong sovereign backing and abundant energy. However, data centres in the region must now confront regional conflict, as gulf-based data centres have been targeted as perceived extensions of US-aligned infrastructure.

## Site acquisition structures are changing

Growing complexity is changing how sites are acquired, funded and developed. Few organisations can independently identify, secure, power, finance and operate large-scale developments, so collaborative models are increasingly important. Commercial models are evolving:

**Joint ventures and strategic partnerships** combine land, development capability, power access, supply chain buying power, operating expertise and institutional capital, allowing participants to share risk and accelerate delivery. Careful thought must be given to governance, deadlock resolution and how different contributions are valued and protected over the life of the venture, particularly where one party's contribution is front-loaded while another's accrues over time.

**Vendor financing arrangements** bridge the gap between land acquisition and project maturity. Deferred consideration, milestone payments, overage mechanisms and seller loans can reduce upfront capital requirements while aligning seller and developer interests.

**Leasing structures** are adapting to the evolving data center market. Build-to-suit arrangements, powered shell deliveries and phased energisation schedules have become standard in many regions as tenants seek to derisk deployment timelines while landlords manage infrastructure commitments. Sale-and-leaseback structures let operators recycle capital from stabilised assets into land acquisition, power procurement and AI-related infrastructure while retaining operational control through long-term leases. Data sovereignty considerations must be taken into account when selecting structures.

**Forward funding and forward commitment structures** bring institutional capital in much earlier than traditional real estate models, with investors funding development against agreed milestones or committing in advance to acquire completed assets. They parallel build-to-rent and purpose-built student accommodation, where investors fund development against pre-agreed specifications and milestones. Added complexity lies in defining completion and handover standards for highly technical facilities, including Tier III or IV certification, power usage effectiveness (PUE) thresholds and customer-ready fit-out requirements.

**Equipment manufacturer financing and lease backstops** are an increasingly important feature in some regions. Critical equipment manufacturers now act as financing parties for personal property, offering lease financing, deferred payment and equipment-as-a-service models that reduce upfront capital requirements. Some also provide credit backstops for tenant lease obligations, guaranteeing a portion of rent or providing a standby letter of credit, so that operators with thinner balance sheets can secure premises from institutional landlords. Structuring these backstops requires careful attention to the interplay between the primary lease, the backstop agreement and any equipment financing, including subordination, cure rights and remedies on tenant default.

Successful site acquisition is no longer simply about securing land, and the line between site selection and transaction structuring is increasingly blurred. Winning sites will be those where capital, infrastructure, community benefit and expertise can be brought together most effectively.

stories.summary: STTGDC has obtained a US$590 million green loan to fund the fit-out and operation of its Tokyo data center campus, comprising two facilities—STTGDC TYO1 and STTGDC TYO2—that will collectively deliver 70.8 MW of IT capacity. STTGDC, a global colocation data center provider, has secured a US$590 million green loan facility to finance the fit-out and operation of its Tokyo data center campus.The campus, comprising STTGDC TYO1 and STTGDC TYO2, is located in Goodman Business Park in Inzai City, Greater Tokyo area. It will provide a combined 70.8 MW of IT capacity and will cater to hyperscalers, cloud service providers, and enterprises in Japan.Standard Chartered acted as Lead Coordinator for the financing. Standard Chartered and Société Générale served as Green Loan Coordinators.Nelson Lim, Group Chief Financial Officer, STTGDC, stated that the financing reflects the strength of their Japan platform. It also shows the confidence of their banking partners in the Tokyo campus's quality and long-term potential. Lim added that the green-loan structure aligns their financing strategy with the environmental performance of the assets.Kiyoshi Maeda, Chief Executive Officer – Japan, STTGDC, said the Tokyo campus is central to their long-term commitment to Japan. It strengthens their ability to support customers as their cloud, AI, and digital infrastructure requirements grow. Maeda noted that customers need infrastructure that can scale while delivering resilience and efficiency.The facility was structured in accordance with the Green Loan Principles. It links financing to defined environmental eligibility criteria. These include data centers attaining an agreed green building certification and achieving a design Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) ratio of 1.3 or below.STTGDC TYO1, the company's first operational data center in Japan, has achieved LEED Gold certification. It aims to achieve an annualized PUE of less than 1.25. Its closed-loop cooling system is designed to minimize operational water use, with no ongoing consumption during normal operations.The facility has obtained ISO 22301, ISO 27001, and ISO/IEC 20000 certifications. It complies with Japan Data Center Council guidelines. STTGDC TYO1 has maintained carbon-neutral operations for Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions since commencing operations. It continues to pursue renewable-energy procurement and improvements in energy efficiency.STTGDC TYO2 is being developed to support high-density AI and accelerated-computing workloads. It includes provision for future liquid-cooling deployment. This facility is also targeting TIA-942-C Design Certification and LEED Gold.

stories.title: SoleCrypt ups size of planned data center campus in Bizerte, Tunisia
stories.summary: First 7MW phase due live in early 2028, to host Vera Rubin GPUs
stories.content:
SoleCrypt has grown the size of a planned data center in Tunisia and provided details on the project timelines.

The company last week announced plans for the SoleCrypt AI Campus in Bizerte.

The first 7MW of the planned 40MW campus will be designed to host Nvidia’s HGX Rubin NVL8 hardware. The first phase, designed to deploy 1,728 Nvidia Rubin GPUs, could go live in early 2028.

Full details haven’t been shared, but the project will reportedly be located approximately 3.6 km (2.23 miles) from the Medusa subsea cable landing site in Bizerte, via a routed fiber path.

SoleCrypt said the development is supported by a dedicated 60MW solar and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project across 100 hectares, some 525km (326 miles) away in Tozeur.

Launched in 2022, SoleCrypt focuses on developing data centers powered by solar assets. The company previously outlined plans to develop a 20MW data center in Bizerte.

SoleCrypt signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Safozi, a Tunisian cloud and data infrastructure provider, late last year.

The first phase of the Medusa cable, linking Marseille in France and Bizerte in Tunisia, went live earlier this year.

stories.title: First building at Project Jupiter data center campus in New Mexico topped out
stories.summary: Structural work on first building complete, three more to go
stories.content:
The first phase of Project Jupiter, a large-scale data center campus in New Mexico being developed by Stack and Oracle, has been topped out.

Clayco and Kiewit New Mexico Co. this week announced the topping out of the first portion of the Project Jupiter data center campus in Doña Ana County, New Mexico, placing the final structural beam atop the facility and completing the building’s primary structural framework.

Oracle and Stack chose a Clayco and Kiewit joint venture as general contractors on the first 855,000-square-foot (79,432 sqm) portion of the data center campus, with the project breaking ground in October 2025.

“As part of our commitment to building to make life better, Clayco is proud to reach this benchmark moment in the construction of Project Jupiter, ultimately helping meet America’s rapidly growing demand for sustainable, advanced technology infrastructure,” said Ryan McGuire, Clayco’s president of construction and compute. “As the need for advanced technological facilities grows, so does Clayco’s commitment to delivering high-quality data center projects that not only support billions in community investments and the creation of thousands of skilled jobs, but that utilize on-site power generation and sustainable water technologies to minimize impacts to local electric grids and water systems.”

Announced last year, the campus will span 1,400 acres with four data center buildings, micro-grid facilities, natural gas power plants, a battery storage center, and a desalination plant. Oracle will occupy the campus once construction is complete, and will use it to host AI infrastructure for OpenAI.

The site could total up to 2.5GW at full build-out, though the project has reportedly faced challenges around securing a natural gas connection.

“Reaching this milestone reflects the extraordinary coordination and commitment of the teams bringing Project Jupiter to life,” said Mike Casey, COO of Stack Infrastructure. “From the outset, our focus has been to develop critical digital infrastructure in a way that delivers lasting value for Doña Ana County. Project Jupiter demonstrates how infrastructure at this scale can advance technological innovation while supporting local jobs, strengthening the regional economy, and responsibly managing energy and water resources. We are proud to work alongside Oracle, Clayco, Kiewit, and our local partners as we move this important project forward.”

The companies noted that no public drinking water will be used for data center cooling or fuel-cell operations. The site will use non-potable well water, purchased under contract from an existing New Mexico water-rights holder, for the initial, one-time fill of its four closed-loop, non-evaporative cooling systems. On-site Bloom Energy fuel cells will power a campus microgrid and also rely on non-potable water.

Clayco is a real estate development and construction firm. Kiewit is a North American construction and engineering organization.

“Kiewit is thrilled to reach this significant milestone in partnership with Clayco, Stack Infrastructure, and Oracle,” said Tyler Nordquist, SVP, Kiewit New Mexico Co. “Projects of this scale are built through trust, collaboration, and an unwavering commitment to safety. Together with our partners, we’re focused on delivering quality construction that supports our client’s vision and creates lasting value for the community.”

“Together with our partners, we are building responsibly—investing in the energy infrastructure needed to protect local ratepayers and grid reliability, using closed-loop cooling systems designed to significantly reduce water consumption, and creating meaningful career opportunities and lasting economic value for Doña Ana County,” said Mahesh Thiagarajan, EVP, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. “We are pleased to work alongside our partners as we build the Project Jupiter data center to meet the growing nationwide customer demand for secure, reliable AI infrastructure.”

stories.title: AirTrunk secures AU$4.25 billion green loan for Sydney data center campus
stories.summary: Current expansion phase for SYD3 site due live in 2028
stories.content:
APAC data center firm AirTrunk has secured billions of dollars to fund development of one of its campuses in Sydney, Australia.

The company this week announced it has secured an AU$4.25 billion ($2.989bn) green loan to fund the continued development of its SYD3 campus in Western Sydney.

A consortium of 32 local and international financial institutions backed the green loan. The deal brings the company’s total committed debt financing to \~AU$38.4 billion (\~US$26.9 billion) globally, including more than AU$19.8bn (US$13bn) across its Australian projects.

First announced in 2021, the company filed to develop the project in 2023. Set on 8.3 hectares, SYD3 could total 400MW at full build-out across 42 data halls and 70,000 sqm (753,475 sq ft) of technical space.

Construction of the expanded SYD3 development is underway, with completion expected by mid-2028.

Tom Mackellar, VP of origination & market expansion, said: “SYD3 is a long-term investment in Western Sydney and Australia’s digital capability, backed by the confidence of leading Australian and international banks. The green financing also reflects our view that sustainability should be built into how digital infrastructure is funded and delivered. We’re focused on responsible growth that creates lasting value for communities in the regions where we operate.”

The facility is structured as a green loan with margin adjustments. Construction measures include the use of lower-carbon steel and concrete, as well as a target to divert at least 90 percent of non-hazardous construction waste from landfill.

AirTrunk said any contributions from the margin savings on the facility will be directed to AirTrunk’s social impact program to support local charities working across STEM education, digital equity, biodiversity and conservation, sustainable innovation and disaster relief.

AirTrunk’s Australian platform spans five campuses, with more than 1.2GW of capacity. SYD1 opened in 2017, with SYD2 launching in 2021.

Founded in 2018, AirTrunk was acquired by Blackstone and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board for US$16.1bn in 2024 in what was the largest-ever deal in the space at the time.

AirTrunk has data center campuses in operation and development in Sydney and Melbourne in Australia, as well as Singapore; Hong Kong; Johor, Malaysia; and Tokyo and Osaka, Japan. It entered India this year with the acquisition of Indian operator Lumina CloudInfra.

The green loan was underwritten by 14 lead banks: Banco Santander, S.A.; BNP Paribas; Crédit Agricole Corporate and Investment Bank; DBS Bank Ltd.; Deutsche Bank; ING Bank N.V.; Mizuho Bank, Ltd.; MUFG Bank, Ltd.; National Australia Bank Limited; Royal Bank of Canada; Société Générale; Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation; The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited; and United Overseas Bank Limited.

Green Loan Coordinators were: Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation; The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited; and United Overseas Bank Limited. Legal advisers for the transaction were Mallesons and Gilbert & Tobin.

stories.title_zh: 泰国数据中心新草案将提交内阁审议
stories.summary_zh: 泰国数据中心（DC）政策委员会已批准数据中心治理政策草案，该草案将为数据中心的投资和运营建立监管框架，目标是确保该行业高效且可持续的发展。该草案将很快提交内阁审议，因为泰国正努力将自己定位为区域数字基础设施枢纽。

stories.content:
Thailand’s Data Center (DC) Policy Committee yesterday approved the draft policy on data center governance which will be submitted to the Cabinet for consideration soon, according to local reports. The draft policy establishes a regulatory framework for investment and operation of data centers with the goal of ensuring the efficient and sustainable development of the country’s digital economy. The draft policy is reportedly scheduled for Cabinet consideration on 3 November 2026.

The most important draft policy which has so far not been officially stated in Thailand is the definition of a data center in Thai context. The draft policy defines a data center to include buildings, premises, or structures that possess and use electronic equipment to provide services related to the collection, storage, processing, reception, or transmission of data electronically to persons other than affiliated companies, with a minimum electricity requirement of 0.5 megawatts (MW).

The second most important draft policy is the establishment of a one-stop center to coordinate approvals and licensing. The Ministry of Digital Economy and Society has been tasked to develop the TH-DC Dashboard system to consolidate the approval and licensing from various government agencies into a single system. This will facilitate more systematic project status tracking and coordination between agencies.

The third most important draft policy is the establishment of four minimum standards for the data center operators to ensure basic business conditions are met including not impacting the safety of life and property of the public especially the surrounding communities.

The four minimum standards include the following:

- Location and land use, including land use plans and oil reserve storage for electricity generation.
- Connecting the country’s public utility networks, including both the electricity and water systems.
- Environmental standards require the preparation of a Code of Practice (CoP) report.
- Creating economic and social contributions to ensure that investments generate benefits for the country and communities.

### New DC classification

Data centers will be classified into 7 levels based on their power demand, as detailed below:

Level 1: 0–0.5 MW

Level 2: More than 0.5–5 MW

Level 3: More than 5–10 MW

Level 4: More than 10–20 MW

Level 5: More than 20–50 MW

Level 6: More than 50–200 MW

Level 7: 200 MW and above.

Each level will have different levels of requirements based on size and resource needs. Subcommittee 1 is tasked with developing detailed procedures and processes for approval and licensing.

Since the minimum standard requirements are additional requirements to the announcements, regulations, and laws currently used by various agencies, new laws will be drafted or current laws amended before the minimum standards can be enforced. This is expected to take approximately 8–12 months.

#### **Guidelines during transition period**

 At the same time, the new regulations, in principle, cannot be immediately applied retroactively to contractors who have already constructed and obtained licenses in accordance with the law prevailing at the time. Therefore, the committee established guidelines for oversight during the transition period, divided according to four project statuses as follows:

 **1. Data centers that are already in operation.**

 The Ministry of Digital Economy and Society is tasked with drafting legislation to require businesses to comply with the Communities of Practice (CoP) that the Policy Committee will announce. This must be completed within one year, and CoP documents must be submitted through the DC-OSS system according to the specified procedures.

1.  **Data centers that received construction permits before August 11, 2026, and have been completed, are ready to open for service.**

For projects that received construction permits under Form A.1 or were implemented under Section 39 before August 11, 2026, the date the relevant Prime Minister’s Office regulations came into effect, the responsible agencies shall consider approving and granting permits in accordance with the current laws, announcements, and regulations in force.

Agencies must notify the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society of the decision through the DC-OSS system within five days. Once it has been verified that the approval and licensing are complete, the Ministry will notify the operators to begin operations, provided they comply with the CoP (Community of Practice) within 1 year and submit the necessary documents through the DC-OSS system according to the procedures.

1. **Data centers that have received construction permits from August 11, 2026 onwards, or those that have not yet received construction permits.**

 This group of projects will be considered new businesses that must comply with minimum requirements.

1.  **Data centers that are already operational and have plans to expand their power capacity.**

If the system’s capacity is expanded to the point where the total electricity demand increases by more than 20MW, the expanded portion shall be considered a new project and must comply with the same minimum standards.

However, because the projects in the new entrant group and the electricity expansion projects have different progress levels, the committee assigned Subcommittee 1 to consider approval and licensing guidelines for both groups during the transition period and to complete this within one month.

### One-Stop Service system

 With regards to consideration of new data center projects, the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society has been tasked with expediting the drafting of legislation to integrate the management and regulation of data center operations into a single system. The initial approach will involve soliciting data center investment proposals in rounds and selecting proposals through a pitching process, using a One-Stop Service for Data Centers (DC-OSS) mechanism as a central hub for coordination and data connectivity.

The DC-OSS system will work in conjunction with the TH-DC Dashboard to collect databases, monitor status, track and evaluate project progress, and conduct preliminary project proposal screening before submitting them to the relevant screening committee for consideration and selection according to the criteria to be announced by the Policy Committee.

In addition, the committee assigned Subcommittee 1 to expedite the development of criteria for selecting data center projects, to be submitted to the committee for consideration in accordance with the established procedures.

### Green Data Centers to support Net Zero by 2050

 The guidelines have the objective of supporting investment in data center development in line with the country’s development direction and goals, focusing on the following issues:

- Promoting Green Data Centers supports the development of environmentally friendly data centers to help drive the goal of net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.
- Support the procurement ofresources for internal use, either in part or in whole, to meet the resource requirements of projects.
- Maintain the quality and continuity of service by monitoring and ensuring that operators comply with Service Level Agreements (SLAs).
- To create added economic and social value, promote domestic employment, encourage the use of domestically produced parts and components, and support investment in digital and related industries.
- The establishment of regulatory guidelines and selection criteria for data center investments aims to ensure that the expansion of digital infrastructure proceeds in parallel with the management of energy, resources, the environment, and economic and social benefits, in order to support the long-term development of Thailand’s digital economy.

The meeting was chaired by Ekniti Nitithanprapas, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance.

Thailand reportedly has about 63 operating facilities, 20 under construction and more than 100 proposed projects with preliminary combined electricity requirements of approximately 3GW.

stories.summary: Paragon Globe Bhd (KL:PGLOBE) on Tuesday received shareholders’ approval for its proposed sale of 65 acres of land in Iskandar Puteri, Johor, to a unit of Singapore-based DayOne Data Centers Ltd for RM398.11 million.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 27): Paragon Globe Bhd (KL:PGLOBE) on Tuesday received shareholders’ approval for its proposed sale of 65 acres of land in Iskandar Puteri, Johor, to a unit of Singapore-based DayOne Data Centers Ltd for RM398.11 million.

The property group said the disposal by its wholly owned subsidiary, PGB Landmark Sdn Bhd, is expected to generate an estimated net pro forma gain of RM187.43 million as it continues to selectively monetise its land bank.

A total of 24 shareholders holding 522.45 million shares voted in favour of the disposal at an extraordinary general meeting, while two shareholders holding 202 shares voted against it. The votes in favour accounted for 99.9999% of the shares voted, the group said in a bourse filing.

Paragon Globe said the disposal is expected to strengthen its financial position. Based on its audited financial statements as at March 31 and assuming the transaction is completed, net assets per share would rise to 89 sen from 64 sen, while gearing would fall to 0.68 times from 1.06 times.

The gearing reduction takes into account a proposed RM56 million repayment of bank borrowings using part of the disposal proceeds.

Of the RM398.11 million in gross proceeds, Paragon Globe said RM146 million has been earmarked for ongoing projects, including Calia Residences by PGB and Kensley Square @ Kensington Parkview. Another RM56 million will be used to partially repay bank borrowings, while RM57.1 million has been set aside for future land bank or property acquisitions.

The land, which is located in Tanjung Kupang, was originally earmarked for the first phase of an industrial development comprising 88 factory units, with an estimated gross development value of RM419.1 million.

“Instead of tying up our cash for years to build factories on this site, we decided it was smarter to accept a good offer on the land. Once completed, the disposal will allow us to put more capital into our ongoing projects, build up our rental-income assets and reduce some borrowings,” said Paragon Globe executive chairman Datuk Seri Edwin Tan Pei Seng in a statement.

“We want to keep growing, but liquidity must always come first,” said Tan, who is the group's largest shareholder via Paragon Adventure Sdn Bhd with a 56.79% indirect stake. He also holds a 0.02% direct stake in the property developer.

As at Sept 28, PGB Landmark had received RM228.91 million — representing 57.5% of the total disposal consideration — under the staged payment structure of the sale and purchase agreement.

The transaction is targeted for completion in the second half of 2027.

Shares of Paragon Globe ended one sen or 1.41% higher at 72 sen on Tuesday, valuing the group at RM537.57 million.

stories.summary: Crusoe, an artificial intelligence infrastructure and cloud platform builder and operator, has announced a strategic partnership with Paraguayan energy and infrastructure developer Araico to build high-performance AI compute infrastructure powered by the Itaipú Hydroelectric Dam. An initial deployment will come online in mid-2027 with a path to scale to 106 MW of IT capacity and […]
stories.content:
Crusoe, an artificial intelligence infrastructure and cloud platform builder and operator, has announced a strategic partnership with Paraguayan energy and infrastructure developer Araico to build high-performance AI compute infrastructure powered by the Itaipú Hydroelectric Dam.

An initial deployment will come online in mid-2027 with a path to scale to 106 MW of IT capacity and long-term options to expand to approximately 280 MW, according to a press release. The facility will be located adjacent to the Itaipú substation, allowing it to draw from one of the largest renewable hydroelectric power sources in the world. The facility will serve both US and Latin American customers through Crusoe Cloud.

“Paraguay’s unique history and geography have enabled one of the most abundant renewable power sources in the world through the Itaipú Hydroelectric Dam. Crusoe’s energy-first strategy is designed precisely to unlock and add value to this kind of power resource through advanced digital infrastructure. On behalf of the whole Crusoe team, we look forward to making this project a success for the people of Paraguay, for our local partners and for Crusoe,” said Cully Cavness, Crusoe Chief Strategy Officer, President, and co-founder.

“Partnering with Crusoe brings world-class AI infrastructure to Paraguay while showcasing our nation’s renewable energy leadership on a global scale,” said Alejandro Zuccolillo, Araico Chief Executive Officer. “By pairing Itaipú’s massive hydroelectric capacity with Crusoe’s ability to build and manage AI infrastructure, we are capturing maximum value from Paraguay’s renewable power right here at home, and transforming our energy abundance into high-tech industrial growth, local jobs, and digital innovation.”

In its Global Data Center Trends 2026 report, CBRE highlighted that Paraguay’s abundant hydroelectric power and agreeable regulatory environment were drawing investors to the South American country.

This will be Crusoe’s first AI cloud deployment in Latin America.

“This partnership between Crusoe and Araico directly unlocks new value from our natural resources. It brings jobs, investment, technology, and innovation to Paraguay, and gives us a scalable model to create meaningful, lasting change for the Paraguayan people. This is an opportunity for Paraguay to establish itself as a regional leader in AI infrastructure,” said Santiago Peña, President of Paraguay.

Data center construction is set for a surge in spending in the next few years. According to Mordor Intelligence, the South America data center construction market is set to grow in value from US$ 5.72 billion in 2026 to US$ 8.88 billion by 2031.

stories.summary: A proposal for a gigawatt-scale off-grid data center campus in Western Australia would rely on on-site natural gas generation paired with a nearby battery energy storage system (BESS). The project represents a rare attempt to build at massive scale entirely outside traditional grid infrastructure in a region with abundant land and energy resources.
stories.why_it_matters: If developed, this project would challenge the prevailing assumption that hyperscale and AI training campuses must anchor to established grid nodes, potentially opening vast new geographies for data center construction across Australia and similar markets. It also tests whether natural gas-plus-BESS hybrid models can satisfy growing sustainability scrutiny from hyperscale tenants and financiers, with implications for how off-grid and carbon-intensive generation are evaluated in future campus developments worldwide.

Plans have been filed for a gigawatt-scale off-grid data center campus in Western Australia.

Gingerah Energy has filed for the Meridien Renewable Energy Hub and Data Centre with the Australian National Environmental Protection Agency’s EPBC portal.

The company is aiming to develop the Frazier Downs pastoral lease, on land located some 100km (62 miles) south of Broome.

Spanning around 27,520 hectares, the project would consist of a 6.7GW renewable energy hub featuring approximately 5.2GW of solar capacity and 1.5GW of wind turbines, supported by 5GW of battery energy storage and around 1.5GW of natural gas firming capacity. This would power a 1GW data center campus and on-site substations.

The first stage, featuring up to 240MW IT load, is anticipated to be progressively constructed and commissioned over two to three years. Construction could reportedly start in 2029, and full build-out is targeted for 2038. The data centers would feature closed-loop cooling to reduce water use.

“Project Meridien has the potential to become Western Australia’s most significant near-term sustainable AI campus, combining gigawatt-scale data center capacity with dedicated renewable energy infrastructure and potentially the lowest latency connectivity to Singapore of any location in Australia,” said Gingerah Energy founder and CEO, Jap van Hattum. “Our proposition is not to finance and build a multibillion-dollar development ourselves, but to establish an investment-ready infrastructure platform bringing together specialist energy providers, data center developers and anchor customers.”

Gingerah Energy is a joint venture whose partners include Longreach Capital Investment, the Karajarri Traditional Lands Association (KTLA) – the registered native title body for the Karajarri people – and Fugro Exploration (the Australian arm of Dutch geodata company Fugro).

The Karajarri people own the land the project is set to be built on. Gingerah Energy entered into an Indigenous Land Use Agreement for the land two years ago. The site was previously earmarked to be a large-scale renewables-based green hydrogen and ammonia project, with Gingerah set to include geothermal power generation capacity.

stories.title: Hyperscale AI growth drives scramble for data center power
stories.summary: Hyperscale AI expansion is creating an unprecedented demand for electricity, straining existing power grids across North America. Data center developers are increasingly building or co-developing their own power generation to secure supply.
stories.content:
Hyperscale AI data center developers are facing significant power challenges as their investment and demand for electricity surge, according to Industrial Info Resources (IIR). Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, and Google's combined data center spending is projected to exceed $700 billion this year, up from $64 billion in 2018.This digital infrastructure buildout indicates a structural, multiyear theme, said Shane Mullins, an analyst with IIR. He noted 12 consecutive months of new project announcements with consistently elevated spending.The rapid expansion has also led to growing community resistance, with over 500 data center moratoria recorded across 42 US states. New Jersey and Michigan account for 41 and 36 moratoria respectively.New York has temporarily banned new data centers larger than 50 MW, while Texas paused new grid interconnections for approximately 200 GW of requests. Mullins stated that $130 billion in projects were rejected in Q1 2026 alone.Despite opposition, the AI infrastructure buildout continues, with over $400 billion per month in newly announced data center projects globally since April 2026. Cumulative capital expenditure has surpassed $7 trillion.The US and Canada alone have a pipeline of roughly $4.75 trillion, encompassing more than 4,250 planned or in-progress data center projects. Texas contributes nearly $1.25 trillion to this total.More than 400 GW of new data center load is in planning globally, with almost 100 US sites designed for at least 1 GW. Operational data center load in the US has increased from 23 GW in 2023 to 53 GW currently, with another 42 GW approved or under construction.US data center electricity demand could reach 125 GW by 2030, up from 35 GW in 2024. Grid planners' forecasts for additional electricity demand within a decade have climbed sevenfold, from 24 GW in 2022 to 166 GW by 2025.Developers are increasingly opting to build, own, or co-develop power generation. Gas turbines are preferred for projects requiring more than 1 GW, but manufacturers like GE Vernova, Mitsubishi Power, and Siemens Energy are sold out through 2029, with orders extending to 2031.IIR estimates $228 billion in new natural gas power plant projects are underway to meet the AI data center demand gap. Britt Burt, an IIR analyst, noted natural gas is the fastest, most reliable path to new dispatchable capacity.Nuclear energy is also seeing renewed interest, with 111 projects valued at $311.4 billion, including 61 small modular reactors (SMRs). Solar paired with battery energy storage systems (BESS) is another fast-growing combination, with 701 BESS projects worth almost $200 billion.Interconnection delays, labor and equipment shortages, grid congestion, limited transmission capacity, and community opposition are constraints shaping every energy source. Burt highlighted that AI and data center buildout are driving electricity demand growth not seen in a generation.

stories.content:
Revenue is up 1.6% at US$134.5 million from US$132.4 million in the year-ago period

\[SINGAPORE\] The manager of Digital Core Real Estate Investment Trust (Reit) expects its distribution per unit (DPU) to rise to between US$0.0415 and US$0.0425 for 2027.

This is about 17 per cent higher at the midpoint than its current DPU of US$0.036, noted its CEO John Stewart in an earnings call on Tuesday (Oct 27).

It is the first formal forward guidance the pure-play data centre Reit has given regarding its DPU.

Driving the increase in the DPU is the beginning of its Linton Hall lease, which will begin its 10-year lease starting in December, as well as the full year’s contribution from its manager asset swap with Digital Realty, said Stewart.

He noted that the Linton Hall facility – which has been vacant since a previous tenant left in June 2025 – is “on track and on budget” to begin operations soon.

In addition to the DPU guidance, the Reit manager also guided cash rental reversion to be in the positive mid-single digits in 2027.

Digital Core Reit also expects portfolio occupancy to be about 50 basis points over or under its current value. In addition, it forecasts the average interest rate to be between 3.25 per cent and 3.75 per cent.

The guidance comes off the back of a proposed major portfolio revamp that marked its entry into Singapore, and grew its presence in Japan alongside its divestments in three North American assets.

The Reit’s manager noted then that the sale of interests in its Los Angeles, Toronto and Northern Virginia facilities is expected to generate gross proceeds of some US$315.9 million.

The partial-interest purchases of data centres in Singapore and Osaka is estimated to represent a total investment of around US$176 million, the manager said at the time.

## Dip in 9M results due to lack of contribution

Distributable income of the Reit fell 1.1 per cent to US$34.8 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from US$35.2 million in the year-ago period.

Revenue rose 1.6 per cent year on year to US$134.5 million from US$132.4 million, the manager said in a Tuesday (Oct 27) bourse filing.

Net property income (NPI) of the pure-play data centre Reit stood at US$64.8 million, down 4.3 per cent from US$67.7 million previously.

Stewart attributed the dip in NPI to the lack of contribution from the Linton Hall facility.

Linton Hall contributed to the NPI for six months in 2025 and zero in 2026, he added.

As at Sep 30, the Reit had 11 data centres and assets under management worth US$1.9 billion, with 65 per cent in North America, 24 per cent in Germany and 11 per cent in Japan.

Portfolio weighted average of leasing expiry (Wale) stood at four years, while in-service portfolio occupancy stood at 97 per cent.

Following the portfolio change – which Stewart expects to be completed in the fourth quarter – the Reit’s pro forma assets under management will dip slightly to US$1.8 billion, with 52 per cent of its assets in North America, 26 per cent in Germany, 18 per cent in Japan and 4 per cent in Singapore.

In addition, the number of data centres the Reit will have under its belt will fall to 10, while Wale will stand at five years with a 99 per cent occupancy.

Unitholders approved the deal in an extraordinary general meeting on Oct 22, with 99.92 per cent of the votes cast in favour.

Units of Digital Core Reit ended Tuesday flat at US$0.44, before the announcement.

stories.title: Seatrium and Karpowership plan to build floating power, data centers in Singapore
stories.summary: Seatrium and Karpowership signed an MOU to develop integrated floating platforms combining power generation and data center infrastructure in Singapore. The partnership aims to leverage Seatrium's offshore engineering expertise with Karpowership's floating power plant technology to address land scarcity and power constraints for digital infrastructure expansion.
stories.why_it_matters: Singapore faces severe land and power limitations that have constrained data center growth, with the government imposing moratoriums and strict capacity caps. Floating infrastructure offers a novel workaround to these constraints, potentially allowing Singapore to expand its digital economy without consuming scarce land resources. If proven viable, this model could be replicated in other land-constrained APAC hubs like Hong Kong and Tokyo, reshaping how the region approaches data center site selection.

stories.summary_zh: Seatrium 与 Karpowership 签署谅解备忘录，计划在新加坡开发集成 floating power 与 data center 的浮动平台。该合作将结合 Seatrium 的 offshore engineering 专业能力与 Karpowership 的 floating power plant 技术，以应对数字基础设施扩张面临的土地稀缺和电力约束问题。

stories.content:
Seatrium Limited, a Singapore-based engineering company specializing in offshore, marine, and energy infrastructure solutions, has entered into a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Karpowership, an operator of floating power plants, to build out floating power and infrastructure solutions in Singapore.

As stated in a press release, Seatrium and Karpowership intend to create an integrated platform, combining infrastructure development, financing, engineering, construction, and operations, to develop and deploy floating infrastructure that may include powerships, floating data centers, turbine-based or hybrid vessels, and floating nuclear solutions.

The collaboration brings together Seatrium’s offshore engineering, procurement, construction, and systems integration capabilities and Karpowership’s expertise in developing, financing, owning, and operating floating power and digital infrastructure.

“As demand for power and digital infrastructure accelerates, our industry has an opportunity to develop new solutions that combine speed of deployment, flexibility and scale. Building on our longstanding strategic relationship with Karpowership, we aim to strengthen Singapore’s status as a hub for next-generation floating energy and digital infrastructure, using the best-available technologies, including hydrogen-ready power generation,” said Chris Ong, Seatrium Chief Executive Officer.

The companies have said that in the coming months they will progress discussions toward forming a joint venture, subject to the negotiation and execution of definitive agreements and the necessary approvals.

“Karpowership has pioneered floating power infrastructure worldwide, expanding its capabilities to deliver gigawatt-scale, behind-the-meter power solutions for the most developed markets, floating digital infrastructure and turnkey data centre solutions spanning the entire value chain. Karpowership’s decades-long relationships with OEMs and technology partners, including Seatrium, now extend to a global network of commercial partnerships, including with hyperscalers,” said Orhan Remzi Karadeniz, Karpowership CEO.

The MOU comes at a time when Singapore’s peak electricity demand is set to grow between 2.4 and 4.8 percent annually to reach up to 11.4 GW by 2031, according to the Energy Market Authority. Demand, the authority says, is being driven by strong economic growth, transport electrification, and the expansion of energy-intensive sectors such as semiconductor manufacturing and data centers.

stories.content:
STTGDC, a global colocation data center provider, has announced that it has secured a US$ 590 million green loan facility to finance the fit-out and subsequent operation of STTGDC TYO1 and STTGDC TYO2, the two buildings comprising its data center campus in Japan. Located in Goodman Business Park in Inzai City, in the Greater Tokyo area, the campus will provide a combined 70.8 MW of IT capacity. It will cater to hyperscalers, cloud service providers and enterprises in Japan.

The financing was supported by Standard Chartered, which acted as Lead Coordinator, alongside Mizuho Bank, OCBC, Société Générale and UOB. Standard Chartered and Société Générale also acted as Green Loan Coordinators.

“This financing reflects the strength of our Japan platform and the confidence of our banking partners in the quality and long-term potential of the Tokyo campus,” said Nelson Lim, Group Chief Financial Officer, STTGDC. “It provides the capital foundation to advance the campus while maintaining a disciplined approach to growth. Importantly, the green-loan structure aligns our financing strategy with the environmental performance of the assets we develop, reinforcing how sustainability is integrated into our capital allocation and investment decisions.”

“The Tokyo campus is central to our long-term commitment to Japan and strengthens our ability to support customers as their cloud, AI and digital infrastructure requirements grow,” said Kiyoshi Maeda, Chief Executive Officer – Japan, STTGDC. “Customers need infrastructure that can scale with their ambitions while delivering the resilience and efficiency required for mission-critical operations. Through STTGDC TYO1 and STTGDC TYO2, we are building that capacity in one of Japan’s established data center markets and creating a strong platform for our continued growth in the country.”

STTGDC says that the facility was structured in accordance with the Green Loan Principles, and links financing to defined environmental eligibility criteria. These include the data centers attaining an agreed green building certification and achieving a design Power Usage Effectiveness ratio of 1.3 or below.

STTGDC TYO1, STTGDC’s first operational data center in Japan, has achieved LEED Gold certification and aims to achieve an annualized Power Usage Effectiveness of less than 1.25. Its closed-loop cooling system is designed to minimize operational water use, with no ongoing water consumption during normal operations. The facility has obtained ISO 22301, ISO 27001 and ISO/IEC 20000 certifications and complies with Japan Data Center Council guidelines. STTGDC says that since commencing operations, STTGDC TYO1 has maintained carbon-neutral operations for Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, while continuing to pursue renewable-energy procurement and improvements in energy efficiency. Meanwhile, STTGDC TYO2 is being developed to support high-density AI and accelerated-computing workloads, with provision for future liquid-cooling deployment. It is also targeting TIA-942-C Design Certification and LEED Gold.

stories.title: CDC says it achieved 2030 net-zero target four years early
stories.summary: CDC Data Centres says it achieved its 2030 net-zero target four years ahead of schedule, according to its response to a federal parliamentary inquiry. In its response to the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, the data centre operator said it achieved the target in FY26 across its defined emissions target boundary, which covers Scope […]
stories.content:
CDC Data Centres says it achieved its 2030 net-zero target four years ahead of schedule, according to its response to a federal parliamentary inquiry. In its response to the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, the data centre operator said it achieved the target in FY26 across its defined emissions target boundary, which covers Scope 1, Scope 2 and selected Scope 3 emissions.

CDC said its sustainability reporting is prepared in accordance with Australian Sustainability Reporting Standards, including AASB S2, and is independently assured.

The company reported an operational power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.38 in FY26. CDC also reported a water usage effectiveness (WUE) figure below 0.02. The company said it has used closed-loop cooling systems since 2007. These systems use sealed infrastructure in which water is filled once and continuously recirculated for the life of the facility, which CDC said means its facilities do not require ongoing water consumption for primary cooling.

CDC’s response also addressed the regulatory implications of AI infrastructure, arguing that Australia’s Security of Critical Infrastructure (SOCI) framework remains fundamentally fit for purpose but was not designed as an AI governance regime.

The company supported an ongoing review of the framework’s scope to ensure emerging technologies and business models, including neocloud providers, are covered where they perform nationally significant functions or support critical infrastructure.

CDC also called for proportionate, risk-based regulation and measures to avoid overlapping compliance obligations where organisations are already subject to equivalent Commonwealth security frameworks.

On economic contributions, CDC cited modelling it commissioned in 2026 that estimated the company had supported AU$2.5 billion in gross value added through construction since 2007, alongside approximately AU$444 million in annual economic activity and more than 1,600 ongoing jobs across the Australian economy.

The company said community engagement should begin before formal planning assessment and continue throughout a project’s development, with feedback potentially influencing matters such as traffic, construction scheduling, landscaping and environmental management.
